Let the primes be p_1=2<p_2=3<\cdots. We prove that the sequence contains exactly the numbers p^2 with p prime.

First, a_1=2 and a_2=4=2^2. Suppose p^2 occurs, and let q be the next prime after p. From p^2, while the multiplier t satisfies p\le t<q, every prime divisor of t is at most p; hence \ell(pt)=p. Therefore the sequence successively contains
p^2,p(p+1),\ldots,pq.
At pq, \ell(pq)=q. While p\le t<q, we have \ell(t)\le p<q, so the sequence then contains
q(p+1),q(p+2),\ldots,q^2.
Thus, by induction over the primes, every prime square occurs.

Conversely, the displayed terms are all terms between consecutive prime squares p^2 and q^2. In the first block, p(p+r) with 1\le r<q-p has p-adic valuation exactly 1, because p<p+r<q<2p (Bertrand's postulate, with the case p=2 immediate). Hence these terms are not squares. In the second block, q(p+r) with 1\le r<q-p has q-adic valuation exactly 1, since p+r<q, so these terms are not squares. Therefore the only squares in the sequence are p^2 for primes p. Hence the required natural numbers m are exactly the primes.

Let p and q be consecutive primes. Assume p^2 occurs in the sequence. For p\le t<q, every prime divisor of t is at most p, hence \ell(pt)=p. Therefore the recursion moves through
p^2,p(p+1),\ldots,pq.
At pq the largest prime divisor is q. For p<t\le q, all prime divisors of t other than possibly q are at most p<q; hence the recursion moves through
q(p+1),q(p+2),\ldots,q^2.
Since 4=2^2 is present, induction gives p^2 for every prime p.

Now consider any term strictly between p^2 and q^2. It is either pt with p<t<q or qt with p<t<q. In the first case, t<q<2p for p>2 (and p=2 is checked directly), so p\nmid t; thus pt has p occurring to an odd exponent and cannot be a square. In the second case q\nmid t because t<q; hence qt likewise cannot be a square. Thus no term between consecutive prime squares is a square, and 2 is not a square. Therefore the complete answer is
\[
\boxed{m\text{ is prime}}.
\]

Let p<q be consecutive primes. We establish the exact segment of the sequence from p^2 to q^2. If p\le t<q, then every prime divisor of t is at most p, so \ell(pt)=p. Hence, starting at p^2, the recursion gives
p^2,p(p+1),\ldots,pq.
At pq the largest prime divisor is q. For p<t<q, \ell(t)\le p<q, so \ell(qt)=q; consequently the recursion continues as
q(p+1),q(p+2),\ldots,q^2.

Because 4=2^2 is the first prime square, this segment description inductively proves that every p^2, with p prime, appears.

It remains to exclude other squares. Every term strictly between p^2 and q^2 is one of pt or qt with p<t<q. For pt, we have p\nmid t: for p>2, Bertrand's postulate gives q<2p, so t<2p, while p<t; for p=2 the assertion is immediate. Thus p occurs to exponent one modulo the contribution from t, and pt is not a square. For qt, q\nmid t because t<q, so qt is not a square as well. Therefore consecutive prime-square endpoints are the only squares in the sequence; a_1=2 is not one. Hence
\[
\boxed{\{m\in\mathbb N:m^2=a_i\text{ for some }i\}=\{p:p\text{ prime}\}}.
\]
